lines.text: Hi everyone, welcome back to Build with [Treesa|Tree suh]!
If you are starting with UiPath Agent Builder, concepts like prompts, tools, context, memory,
escalations, guardrails and evaluations can feel like a lot at first.
So in this video, I'm going to simplify the complete Agent Builder journey.
We'll start with the basic building blocks of an agent, then see how we give it data,
instructions, knowledge and tools, and finally how we debug, evaluate and deploy it.
By the end of this video, you should have a clear mental model of how an agent is actually built in UiPath.
Let's start with the big picture.
An agent needs instructions, knowledge, capabilities and a way to involve humans when required.
First, we have the Prompt.
The prompt defines the agent's role, goal, instructions, constraints and expected behaviour.
Next are Tools.
Tools allow the agent to interact with the outside world.
Instead of only generating text, the agent can call an API, run an automation,
execute an activity, invoke another agent or connect through an [MCP|M C P] server.
Then we have Context.
Context gives the agent access to relevant enterprise knowledge while it is reasoning.
And we have Escalations,
which allow the agent to involve a human when approval, review or assistance is required.
You'll also see Memory in Agent Builder.
Memory allows the agent to learn from previous executions and reuse relevant past experience in future runs.
So a simple mental model is:
Prompt tells the agent what to do.
Context tells it what it needs to know.
Tools give it the ability to take action.
Memory helps it learn from previous experiences.
And escalations tell it when to involve a human.
Now, where do we actually build all of this?
UiPath Agent Builder gives us two ways to work with an agent: Form View and Canvas View.
Form View gives us a structured configuration experience.
Canvas View gives us a visual, node-based representation of the agent.
The important thing to understand is that these are not two different agents.
They represent the same underlying agent definition.
If you change something in one view, it remains synchronized with the other.
Inside the workspace, we also have areas such as Project Explorer, Data Manager, Errors,
Properties, Development options and Deployment Configuration.
At the bottom, we have some very useful capabilities that we'll come back to later:
Execution Trail, History and Evaluations.
Before making the agent intelligent, we should first define its contract.
What information does the agent receive?
And what information should it return?
That is where Data Manager comes in.
Imagine we are creating an IT support agent.
Inputs could include: a customer [ID|I D], a ticket description, a priority, or some document text.
The outputs might be: a classification, a summary, a recommended action, or a final resolution.
So the flow becomes: application or workflow, to input arguments, to the agent,
to output arguments, and finally to the next application or process.
This is important because an agent shouldn't just return random free-form text
when another system needs to consume the result.
Clearly defined inputs and outputs make the agent much easier to integrate into real automation.
Now we come to one of the most important parts: Prompts.
Think of the system prompt as the operating instructions for your agent.
It should explain:
Who are you? What are you trying to achieve? What constraints should you follow?
When should you use a tool? When should you retrieve context? When should you escalate to a human?
And what should the final response look like?
Then we have the user prompt, which provides the actual task for that particular execution.
For example: Analyse this incident and recommend the next action.
Agent Builder also allows us to reference different capabilities from the prompt.
So instead of writing isolated instructions, we can connect our prompt to inputs,
tools, context, memory, escalations and outputs.
And this is an important prompt-engineering principle for agents:
Don't only tell the agent what it should achieve.
Tell it when and how it should use the capabilities available to it.
This is where an AI agent becomes much more useful than a normal chatbot.
Without tools, the model can reason and generate an answer.
With tools, it can actually do something.
In UiPath, tools can include Integration Service activities, published automations, APIs,
custom integrations, other agents, functions, [MCP|M C P] servers and more.
The basic tool execution loop is simple.
First, the agent decides which tool is required.
Then it prepares the inputs.
It executes the tool.
It reads the result.
And based on that result, it decides what to do next.
For example, imagine an employee asks: Can you check the status of my laptop request?
The agent may decide that it needs to call an asset-management API.
It passes the employee [ID|I D].
The tool returns the request status.
The agent interprets that result and then responds to the employee.
One thing people often underestimate here is the tool description.
A tool description isn't only documentation for developers.
It helps the agent understand what the tool does and when it should use it.
So clear tool names, descriptions, inputs and outputs matter a lot.
Tools help the agent act.
Context helps the agent know.
Imagine an [HR|H R] agent answering questions about company leave policies.
We don't want it to rely only on what the underlying [LLM|L L M] already knows.
We want it to use our actual company policy.
Through Context Grounding, the agent can retrieve relevant enterprise knowledge while reasoning.
That knowledge might come from policies, product documentation,
process documentation, internal knowledge bases or business information.
The flow is essentially: user request, retrieve relevant context,
use enterprise knowledge, and then make a grounded decision.
So one very simple rule to remember is:
Better context leads to better decisions.
Context tells the agent what is relevant right now.
Memory allows it to benefit from what happened before.
UiPath currently provides concepts such as episodic memory and escalation memory.
Episodic Memory helps the agent remember similar previous cases,
including inputs, outputs, outcomes and feedback.
Suppose an agent previously handled a particular type of support request successfully.
When it encounters a similar request later, that previous experience can help guide the new execution.
Escalation Memory is particularly interesting.
Imagine an agent previously encountered an uncertain case and escalated it to a human.
The human resolved it.
If the agent later encounters a sufficiently similar situation,
it can use that previous human decision as useful context.
Memories are organised inside Memory Spaces, and these can be shared across agents.
The broader idea is powerful:
Instead of treating every execution as if the system has never seen anything before,
the agent can learn from relevant past experiences.
But an agent should not always make every decision autonomously.
There are situations where a human should remain involved.
That is where Escalations come in.
An agent might escalate for: approval, review, correction, or exception handling.
For example, imagine an agent processing refund requests.
If the refund is below a certain threshold, perhaps it can continue automatically.
But if the amount is high, we may want a human to approve it before the next action happens.
This is an important concept in agentic automation.
Human-in-the-loop doesn't mean the automation failed.
It means we intentionally designed the system so that AI handles what it can,
while humans retain control over important decisions.
Once agents can take actions, we also need boundaries.
That is where Guardrails become important.
Before allowing a tool to execute, we might want to check:
Is this action allowed? Are the inputs valid? Is sensitive information involved?
Does this require approval? Should this action be logged or monitored?
If the request passes the guardrail, the tool can execute.
If it doesn't, we can block the action or escalate it.
This is especially important when an agent can update systems, send messages,
change records or trigger business processes.
Agent autonomy should never mean unlimited access.
It should mean autonomy inside clearly defined boundaries.
Behind the agent is the model that powers its reasoning.
Agent Builder gives us controls such as the model itself, temperature, maximum tokens and maximum iterations.
Temperature controls how deterministic or creative the generation should be.
For many business processes, lower temperature is usually useful
because we want consistent behaviour rather than creativity.
Maximum tokens controls how much the model can generate in a response.
And maximum iterations controls how many reasoning loops the agent can go through.
That loop might look like:
Think. Use a tool or retrieve context. Observe the result. Think again.
And continue until the task is completed.
But more iterations do not automatically mean a better agent.
We want enough room for reasoning without allowing unnecessary loops.
Finally, building the agent is only the beginning.
Before putting it into production, we need to understand how it behaves.
That's where the Execution Trail becomes extremely useful.
Instead of only looking at the final answer, we can inspect what happened during the run.
What tool did the agent call? What inputs did it send? What context did it retrieve?
What output came back? Where did an error happen?
We can also use History to look at previous executions.
Then we have Evaluations.
This is how we move from: It worked when I tested it once,
to: We have evidence that this agent behaves consistently across different scenarios.
We can create evaluation sets, define expected outcomes, run multiple tests
and improve the prompts, tools and context based on the results.
Once we are satisfied, we can publish and deploy the agent, observe how it behaves in production,
collect feedback and continue improving it.
So if you want one checklist for building an agent in UiPath, think about it in this order:
Define the goal.
Define your inputs and outputs.
Write clear prompts.
Configure the model.
Add the right tools.
Provide the right context.
Use memory where it adds value.
Define escalation paths.
Add guardrails.
Debug the execution.
Evaluate the behaviour.
Then publish, observe and improve.
Because a good agent is not simply an agent that works once.
A good agent is one that behaves reliably across many different real-world situations.
If you found this useful, save the Agent Builder cheat sheet
and share this video with someone who is starting their journey with UiPath agents.
And if you enjoy practical content around UiPath, automation, AI agents and agentic automation,
subscribe to Build with [Treesa|Tree suh].
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next video!
